messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 54
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Parole Officer
  trauma_type: Police violence
  pcl5: 68

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Moral Violation: People misbehaving, Stress: Stress, Somatic (Heart Racing): Own heart racing or pounding
  Threat: Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen, Startle Response: Feeling jumpy or easily startled, Scanning for Danger: I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger
  Memory: Blocked Before Complete: I find myself pushing the memory away before I can fully recall it, Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me, Incomplete Picture: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing
  Negative Appraisals: Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted, Injustice: What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it, Institutional Failure: The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Javier Morales was a 54-year-old parole officer who had spent most of his adult life believing that order, procedure, and professional restraint were what stood between danger and chaos. The incident that brought him to treatment happened during a joint operation at a county holding facility, when he was assisting with the transfer of a parolee he knew to be verbally oppositional but not physically assaultive. What stayed with Javier was not only the force itself, but the moment he realized the officers around him were not stepping in. In the narrow concrete corridor, after a burst of shouting, there was a strange drop into silence before one officer drove the man into the wall and others followed. Javier remembered his own body locking as he shouted for them to stop and was shoved back himself, his chest pounding so hard he could hear it in his ears. Later, complaints went nowhere. Internal channels closed ranks, reports were rewritten, and he was left with the conviction that he had been betrayed by people he had trusted to uphold the law. To him, what happened was not only violent but profoundly unfair, and the institution that should have protected both the detainee and him had failed.

In the weeks afterward, the smallest moments at work began to carry the charge of that corridor. Javier found that when people were misbehaving in the waiting area or acting defiant during meetings, he did not just see routine noncompliance; he felt his whole body brace as if a line had already been crossed. If the office suddenly went quiet after raised voices, he was certain something dangerous was about to happen. Even ordinary stress on a busy day, or the sensation of his own heart starting to race, could flip him into a state of alertness in seconds. He began scanning hallways, doorways, and faces constantly, startling when a file cabinet slammed or someone came up behind him. The triggers were potent because they felt tied to what he now believed about the event: that misconduct escalates while decent people stand by, and that systems meant to contain wrongdoing cannot be relied on.

Those beliefs only hardened as the memory itself became harder to hold. When Javier tried to think through what happened in the corridor, he could get only fragments—the shove, the sound of a body hitting the wall, the pressure in his chest, the unnatural quiet just before the violence. Then he would mentally pull away before the scene fully formed. He told the therapist that it almost felt unreal, “like something that happened in a movie, not to me,” and yet it upset him too much to stay with it. The more he returned to the sense of betrayal and institutional failure, the less coherent the memory felt; it was as if his mind stalled at the point where trust in his colleagues and profession had broken.

At the same time, the incompleteness of the memory fed his sense that something intolerable had happened and never been answered for. Because he could not lay out a full, settled account in his own mind, Javier kept circling the same conclusions: that he had been let down, that the whole thing had been wrong, that no one had made it right. When the memory came in flashes and then cut off, he took that not as distance from the event but as proof of how extreme it had been. What frightened him most was that even now his mind seemed to respond as if the danger were unfinished.

That feeling showed up daily in his work. As a parole officer, he spent hours in government offices, interview rooms, and institutional corridors that too closely resembled the setting of the assault. Because he was constantly scanning for danger and felt especially on edge when things went unusually quiet, he noticed every shift in tone around him. A tense client, a loud exchange between staff, even his own pulse picking up during a stressful caseload review could send him back into hypervigilance. In that state he became more likely to read misbehavior as the beginning of another moral collapse, another moment when someone would abuse power and everyone else would look away. His jumpiness and constant monitoring made those triggers easier to detect, and once detected they seemed to confirm his view that the world around him was unsafe and ethically unstable.

The same vigilance also disrupted his grasp on the memory. When he started to recall the corridor scene, his body reacted first—heart pounding, shoulders tensing, attention sweeping the room—and he would shut the memory down before it became complete. He had come to believe that if he let himself remember the whole thing, he would either lose control or be overwhelmed by how deeply he had been betrayed. At home his wife noticed he was restless and watchful, especially when the house fell suddenly silent. By the time he sought help, Javier was exhausted by living as if danger were always about to break through a pause in the room. What finally brought him in was the fear that he was no longer just remembering one terrible event, but reorganizing his whole life around it. He said he wanted to know whether it was possible to feel like himself at work again without having to ignore what happened or forgive what he still believed was unforgivable.
